headline: Forget the Fluke Boats — I'm Fishing the Rocks After Dark and So Are the Bass
subhead: While the fleet drifts Sloop Channel at noon, the real weight is coming off the jetty rocks and bay mud after sundown.
body_markdown:
Everybody and their brother is out there drifting Sloop Channel at ten in the morning with a white Gulp on a bucktail, and yeah, that's still a decent way to put a fluke in the cooler. But if that's all you're doing this week, you're leaving the good stuff on the table. I've been working the rocks at Short Beach and the north jetty inside Jones Inlet from last light through full dark, and that's where the real bass have been.

Here's why. The ocean side has been sloppy — we're looking at close to four feet of swell rolling in off the Bight, short period, five seconds, ugly and disorganized. That kind of slop doesn't kill the bite, it just pushes it. Bass don't want to fight that wash in daylight when the water's warm and bright. So they've gone nocturnal on us, same as they have from here up through the Sound. Warm shallow water plus a bright July sun equals lockjaw at noon and a green light after the sun drops. I've seen this pattern plenty of Julys — when the shallows heat up, the bigger fish slide into a dusk-to-dawn feed and structure becomes the whole game.

So that's what I've been fishing. Half-hour before sunset to about ten, ten-thirty, working bunker chunks on a fishfinder rig right up against the rocks at the Short Beach jetty, fresh cut bunker if I can get it, frozen if I can't. Slack tide through the start of the outgoing has been the window — bass are sitting in the eddies where the current breaks off the rock face, waiting for whatever gets swept out of the bay. I've also had good luck slinging a black 2-ounce bucktail with a white pork rind trailer along the inlet-side rocks on the last of the incoming, letting it swing with the current and hopping it slow off bottom. Nothing giant — mostly 24 to 32 inches, a few pushing 34 — but steady enough that I'm not complaining, and a lot more consistent than what the daytime surf guys are reporting off the open beach right now.

Now the fluke. I'm not going to tell you it's dead, because it isn't — moving water over structure is still putting fish in the boat, especially through the Jones Inlet channel itself on the last two hours of the ebb, when everything in the bay gets funneled through that cut. Fifteen to twenty-five feet of water, white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a three-quarter ounce bucktail, dragged slow along bottom. But it's a grind — you're picking through a lot of shorts to find keepers, and the bite window is tighter than it was in June. If you're going to fish it, fish the tide change hard and don't waste time on the slack.

The story I'm more interested in right now is the weakfish. They've been building back into South Oyster Bay on these calm, warm evenings, and I flagged this a while back — told you the comeback was real, not just a rumor from one lucky trip. Mud-bottom pockets off Wantagh and the flats behind Freeport are holding them, and the pattern's simple: quiet water, dusk into dark, small soft plastics or bucktails with a glow tail worked slow just off bottom. Nothing heavy — three-eighths to half-ounce jig heads, light drag, because a weakfish's mouth tears if you horse it. They're not huge yet, mostly 16 to 20 inches, but they pull hard and they're a welcome change from staring at fluke shorts all afternoon.

We called the spring tide right last week — said it would flush the inlet hard, pull bait out on the ebb and pull predators in tight behind it on the flood, and that's exactly what set up that jetty bite I've been leaning on. Now we're sliding into the neap around this first-quarter moon, and that changes the math a little. Current's going to go soft. Less push means the bait doesn't get flushed through the cut with the same urgency, so the bass bite may spread out over a longer window instead of firing hard right at the tide change. I'd rather fish more of the tide than chase one perfect thirty-minute stretch.

Bluefish have been a non-event for me personally this week — I haven't seen the bunker pods pushing hard enough along the beach to trigger a real blitz through the inlet, though that can change fast if a school gets pinned against the beach by an easterly wind. Worth a look at first light with a metal lip swimmer if you're already out there, but I wouldn't build a trip around it yet.

Looking ahead, I'd keep leaning on the after-dark program at the rocks as long as this warm, calm stretch holds — that's where the bigger bass are going to keep showing up. If the wind stays out of the south and the ocean settles down some, I might sneak back out to the beach for an early tide, but until then, my rods are staying rigged for chunk and bucktail after the sun goes down. And keep an eye on that weakfish bite in the bay — quiet, warm evenings are exactly what's been building it back, and I don't see a reason for that to slow down this week.
